problem: JEPA-style world models (DINO-WM, V-JEPA-2-AC, PLDM) plan in a learned embedding space, but no systematic study says which design choices (predictor architecture, rollout loss, context, encoder, proprioception, planner, scale) actually drive planning success.
motivation: Latent-space planning promises efficiency by abstracting irrelevant details, and JEPA-WMs are increasingly used for navigation and manipulation. Existing works differ in many entangled choices, so it is unclear what matters and how to build the best model in the family.
key_idea: Run a controlled, one-factor-at-a-time study of training, architecture, encoder, scaling and planner choices for frozen-encoder JEPA world models, then combine the winners into an optimized JEPA-WM that beats DINO-WM and V-JEPA-2-AC.
insight: Planning success is not an automatic consequence of good rollouts. Multi-step rollout loss acts like scheduled-sampling data augmentation (2 steps best in simulation, 6 on DROID), and proprioception helps in simulation. Image encoders with fine object segmentation (DINO) beat video encoders (V-JEPA). Scaling encoder or predictor size helps only on real-world DROID data, not on simulated tasks, and CEM with L2 cost is the most robust planner, while gradient planners only win on smooth Metaworld tasks.
method: JEPA-WM recipe: frozen visual encoder (DINOv2/v3, V-JEPA) plus trainable action/proprio encoders and a ViT predictor trained with an MSE embedding prediction loss and a frame-causal mask
Multistep rollout loss: adds k-step autoregressive losses L_k with truncated BPTT, studied for k=1,2,3,6
Predictor conditioning: compares feature conditioning+sincos, sequence conditioning+RoPE, feature conditioning+RoPE, AdaLN+RoPE, AdaLN-zero+RoPE; AdaLN+RoPE is chosen
Planner study: CEM, a new Nevergrad (NGOpt) planner, Adam and GD, each with L1 or L2 latent cost; CEM L2 is chosen
Scaling/ablations: encoder size S/B/L, predictor depth 3-12, context W 1-14, with/without proprioception, data fraction 2-100%
Proposed optimum: simulation uses DINOv2-S with a depth-6 AdaLN+RoPE predictor, proprioception, 2-step loss and W=3; DROID/Robocasa uses DINOv3-L with a depth-12 predictor and no proprioception
Evaluation metrics: success rate plus embedding error, proprio decoding error and LPIPS, with Spearman correlation analysis against success

setting.backbone: Frozen DINOv2/DINOv3 (also V-JEPA, V-JEPA-2) encoder + trained ViT predictor with AdaLN action conditioning
setting.model_size: ViT-S encoder and depth-6 predictor for simulation; ViT-L encoder and depth-12 predictor for DROID/Robocasa
setting.training_data: Per-environment trajectories: Metaworld (12600 TD-MPC2 trajectories), Push-T (18500), PointMaze (2000), Wall (1920) from DINO-WM datasets; DROID (8000 trajectories) with zero-shot transfer to Robocasa
setting.action_space: continuous low-level robot/agent actions (frameskip 5 in simulation), optimized by MPC planning
setting.simulator: Metaworld, Push-T, PointMaze, Wall, Robocasa, and offline real Franka videos (DROID)
setting.privileged: Goal image observation; for Wall/Maze goals are sampled from a random 2D state sampler, otherwise from expert policy or dataset frames

numbers_note: No embodied-navigation benchmark from the canonical list is used; 'navigation' means 2D Maze/Wall/Push-T tasks. Ablation results appear only in figures, so they are not included.
results: The optimized JEPA-WM beats DINO-WM on all 8 tasks and V-JEPA-2-AC on Robocasa-Reach and DROID (e.g. Wall 78.8 vs 64.1, DROID 48.2 vs 42.9). V-JEPA-2-AC is better on Robocasa-Place (33.1 vs 30.7).
limitations: The deterministic MSE predictor learns a conditional mean and cannot capture multi-modal futures
Simulated tasks are simple and the evaluation is largely offline or simulated, with no real-robot closed-loop control; the study fixes the frozen-encoder setting
Success-rate noise is large (high std on Robocasa and Metaworld), so some conclusions are task-dependent
